Structure-loss paper · urban conflagrations

Trees, fences and wind in urban conflagrations · 2026-10-13

Our 2002–26 record (726 fires), the USGS Carlson record 2002–22 (361) and CAL FIRE inspections 2013–25 (445) · pre-fire tree canopy between neighbouring buildings (two years before each fire), a tree-linked version of the building block, wind over each town while it burned, public fence data, and the big losses in sparse treed housing (Gatlinburg, Black Forest, Bastrop); wind around each fire (25–100 km, whole fire, how unusual for the place, named wind events); new: do losses lean downwind (lost neighbours against the wind direction, real vs rotated wind)

By Carlo Broderick, NCEAS, UC Santa Barbara · started 2026-10-13 16:54 PDT · updated 2026-10-14 17:18 PDT

We asked whether trees, fences or wind explain the fires the building rule gets wrong. The rule: a fire that reaches a block of more than 89 closely spaced buildings can become an urban conflagration (≥ 50 destroyed buildings joined within 30 m); of the 25 fires in our 2002–26 record that reached such a block, 10 did. Trees between the houses do not explain which of those became urban conflagrations, and linking houses through trees does not improve the rule. Wind was strong in most of them. Trees do matter in a different kind of loss: in forested towns like Gatlinburg, many scattered houses burned in a chain carried by the forest. Fences cannot be tested: no public map exists.PA36 (prereg commit 46db1c3). T1 not shown; T2 no better; leak flag on year − 1 → primary canopy year = ignition year − 2. Three records: Carlson 2002–22, our 2002–26 record, CAL FIRE DINS 2013–25.

How to read this page

Biggest block: the largest group of buildings standing before the fire whose centres are within 35 m of a neighbour in the group (about 20 m wall to wall). Urban conflagration: at least 50 destroyed buildings in one connected patch, each within 30 m (centre to centre) of another destroyed building in the patch. Gap canopy: pre-fire tree cover in the 30 m square between two neighbours. Hover any dot, cell or heading for details; switch to Technical for methods.

Added 2026-10-14 17:07 PDT · updated 2026-10-14 17:18 PDT

Do losses lean downwind?

No. Across all three records, a building next to a destroyed one was lost about as often when it sat downwind of it as when it sat upwind. In a typical fire, neighbours downwind were lost 73.4 % of the time and neighbours upwind 74.0 % (our 2002–26 record, average over 159 fires). The difference, −0.5 points, is well inside what made-up wind directions give, and the ranges rule out a downwind lean larger than about 2 points in any record, far below the 12 points IBHS reported for Eaton and Palisades with a different measure. Wind clearly drives fires into towns (panels below); this panel finds no sign that it decides which neighbour of a lost house burns next.
S1 (pre-registered primary): mean per-fire lean (share destroyed among neighbours ≤ 60 m downwind of a destroyed building − share upwind, ±45° sectors), R1 −0.51 (−2.23 to +1.15), R2 −0.54 (−2.08 to +1.05), R3 −0.58 (−2.82 to +1.82), 2,000 fire-bootstrap draws; rotated-wind p 0.59 / 0.54 / 0.67. Pre-registered verdict: can't tell (same sign, bars not met) (no record meets the downwind or upwind bar; the ±2-point equivalence bar is narrowly missed, lower bounds −2.2 / −2.1 / −2.8).
Downwind: the direction the wind blows toward (a wind from the north-east carries heat and embers to the south-west).
Bearing: the compass direction from one building to another, measured clockwise from north.
Rotated wind check: the same count repeated 999 times with the wind turned to a random direction, to see how often a made-up wind gives as large a result as the real one.
Downwind quarterCrosswind quartersUpwind quarterDestroyed house
How to read the comparison: when two neighbours are both lost, each sits downwind of the other in one direction and upwind in the other, so those pairs count the same on both sides. The test therefore asks where the survivors next to lost buildings sit: more often upwind of the losses (a downwind lean) or not.
Destroyed–destroyed ordered pairs are symmetric (each appears once downwind and once upwind), so p_down − p_up depends only on destroyed–survivor pairs: Σ destroyed-downwind = Σ destroyed-upwind = 97,556 pairs in R2; denominators 112,672 vs 112,350.

How this panel was checked
  • Pre-registered before any number (docs/ledger.d/2026-10-14-2355-downwind-lean--prereg.md); one later amendment added two checks (observation-based map only; fires where two maps agree) after the main run showed the 4 km map's direction was off for Tubbs and Marshall. Neither changes the answer.
  • Like for like: same statistic, distance (60 m), sectors and fire rule in all three full records, side by side. Fires without a town wind reading (fewer than 100 buildings nearby) are left out: our record 102 fires holding 1,705 destroyed buildings, CAL FIRE 24 incidents holding 583.
  • Denominators: building pairs within 60 m of a destroyed building, by sector; every share in the hovers names its pairs. Each fire counts once in the headline; the all-pairs version (big fires weigh more) and the version without the largest fire (Camp) are in the hovers and give the same answer.
  • Uncertainty from the independent unit: fires resampled 2,000 times; the rotated wind check keeps each town's real loss map and layout fixed and only turns the wind, so street and valley directions cannot create a false lean.
  • Town layout: a second measure compares the direction of lines between lost buildings with the direction of lines between all buildings in the town before the fire (streets, valleys). No record shows lost pairs lining up with the wind more than the layout does.
  • Wind direction is uncertain: burn-window directions from the 4 km simulation (CONUS404) are within 45° of the coarse global map (ERA5) for 271 of 327 fires; the two observation-based maps (HRRR, RTMA) agree for 228 of 243. Every alternative wind source gives the same answer (checks table).
  • Bearings use true north: building points were converted from the national map grid (whose north is about 14° off in California) before any angle was taken.
  • The side the fire came from gives a lean as small as the wind's, so this test cannot separate the two; neither shows a lean.
  • Claims match the evidence: 'no lean shown' with ranges that exclude a downwind lean above about 1–3 points depending on record. This is not a contradiction of IBHS (destroyed vs damaged, 60 m centres vs 3 m wall gaps, two fires); we cannot yet test their exact measure, which needs footprints and wall-to-wall gaps.
  • Fire weather is a description only here; it is never part of a definition or a model input.

Wind around the fire: did it separate urban conflagrations? (PA53)

Words used here. Sustained wind: the wind averaged over the hour; gust: the strongest short burst. ERA5: a global hourly weather map from the European weather centre, one value per cell of about 28 × 22 km, the same product for every year 2002–2026, so fires from different years can be compared fairly. Percentile: where a value ranks among many; the 99th percentile is higher than 99 of every 100 values.

The owner's question: is it enough to read the wind in one cell over the town at the moment it burned? Here we zoom out, with one weather map (ERA5) for every fire: the windiest spot within 25, 50 and 100 km, how windy the whole region was, how many windy hours the whole fire had, how unusual the wind was for that place, and whether it was a recognised wind event.

Did the 10 fires (our record) that became urban conflagrations have broader or stronger wind than the 15 whose big block did not? Pre-set reading: not shown. Example, windiest spot within 100 km while the town burned, our record: median 10.4 vs 11.2 m/s (p 0.98). Some single rows have p below 0.05 (Within 100 km, whole fire in CAL FIRE inspections (DINS), all incidents), but none holds in all three records and none survives the adjustment for testing eight measures. Hours of sustained wind of 10 m/s or more over the whole fire (pre-registered) are zero for almost every fire in this coarse map (median 0 h in both groups, all three records), so that row is left out of the table; hours with gusts of 20 m/s or more stand in for it. Recognised wind events (counted of fires with a known answer, became vs did not): Carlson 2002–22: 8 of 8 vs 14 of 15; Our full 2002–26 record: 10 of 10 vs 14 of 15; CAL FIRE inspections: 7 of 7 vs 4 of 7.

What it suggests: both groups mostly burned in strong regional wind; wind decides that fire reaches the town, but these broader measures do not tell which big blocks became urban conflagrations. With 10 against 15 fires only large differences could show, so this is 'not shown', not 'no effect'.

PA53 prereg docs/ledger.d/2026-10-14-0425-wind-context--prereg.md. ERA5 hourly (Earth Engine ECMWF/ERA5/HOURLY, native 0.25° grid). Burn window = PA41 window (FIRMS-timed town burn ± 12 h). Whole fire = ignition → last FIRMS detection within 30 km before a ≥ 3-day gap (cap 30 d). Circles: cells intersecting the circle; area mean cell-area weighted. Medians with exact 95% intervals, two-sided Mann-Whitney; Holm over the 8 primary measures in p31x_compare.csv. Checks: one fire per regional event (r100_wmax_bw, ours: p 0.86, n 9 vs 6); 2014–2026 only (p 0.52, n 9 vs 5).

How this panel was checked
  • One weather map (ERA5) for every fire and every measure in this table, so no comparison crosses a product change (PA41's finer town measures switch source in 2024 and are kept out).
  • Three full records side by side, with fire counts in every cell; groups are 7 to 15 fires, so only large differences could show.
  • Eight measures tested: the Holm-adjusted p is in each p hover. Sensitivity: one fire per regional wind event (October 2007, October 2017, September 2020 and January 2025 each count once): p 0.86; 2014–2026 only: p 0.52 (windiest spot within 100 km, our record).
  • Medians, not means, so one extreme fire (Eaton, Marshall) cannot carry a group.
  • ERA5 reads peaks low and is coarse (about 28 × 22 km): it describes the regional wind, not the gust in a street. It is the same for both groups.
  • Wind is described here; it is never part of the definition and never a model input.

Zooming out: town cell → 100 km, burn hours → whole fire

Read each row left to right: the wind in the town's cell, then the windiest spot within 25, 50 and 100 km while the town burned, the region-wide average at its peak, the windiest spot over the whole fire, and the count of gusty hours over the whole fire. Darker = windier. A bigger circle can only find an equal or windier spot; the point is how much: in our record the windiest spot within 100 km was a median 2.6 m/s windier than the town's own cell (355 fires). Hours of sustained wind of 10 m/s or more almost never show in this coarse map (it smooths peaks), so the gust-hour column carries the whole-fire signal. The two median rows (became vs did not) look alike.

ERA5 0.25°, hourly. Circles: max over cells intersecting the circle. Region-wide = max over hours of the cell-area-weighted circle mean. Whole fire: ignition → FIRMS end rule; hour counts use the max over the fire-area cells (cells holding ≥ 1 FIRMS detection within 30 km, plus the town cell). Hour cells shaded by share of fire hours. Colour domain 0–16 m/s.

Added 2026-10-13 22:18 PDT · updated 2026-10-14 17:18 PDT

How unusual was the wind for that place?

Each dot is a fire in our record; the black bar is the group median. A fire at 99 had a fire-day wind stronger than 99 of every 100 comparable spans at that same place in 1991–2020 (for a one-day burn, about a 1-in-100-day wind). Both groups sit high: medians 96 (became) and 95 (did not), p 0.85; Carlson p 0.47; CAL FIRE p 0.80. What it suggests: these fires mostly burned their towns on unusually windy days for the place, but how unusual does not separate the two groups.

ERA5 daily max of hourly sustained 10 m wind at the town cell (local standard days). Fire value = max over the k local days touched by the burn window; percentile against all k-day running maxima 1991–2020 (k-day spans, so a long burn is not favoured); season = spans centred within ± 30 days of the fire date. 1-in-N days = k / P(span ≥ fire value). Climatology completeness: minimum share of days present 1.000.

Added 2026-10-13 22:18 PDT · updated 2026-10-14 17:18 PDT

Known wind events, fire by fire

Which fires were known wind events? Of the 25 fires in the two groups (our record), 24 of the 25 with a known answer were recognised wind events by our pre-set rule. A pressure difference between coast and inland is what drives these winds: the bigger the inland high, the harder air pours toward the coast. A Red Flag Warning is the National Weather Service saying fire will spread fast (wind plus dry air and fuels).

Offshore pairs (ERA5 MSLP at airport cells): LAX−DAG / LAX−TPH (CA < 35.5°N), SFO−WMC / SFO−RNO (CA ≥ 35.5°N), PDX−DLS (OR, WA); min over burn window, percentile among all hours 1991–2020; strong ≤ 1 %, moderate ≤ 5 %. Warnings: IEM json/vtec_events_bypoint.py at the town point (public and fire-weather zones), FW.W, HW.W, EW.W, WI.Y overlapping the burn window; archive from 2005-10-01. No historical Santa Ana Wildfire Threat Index archive is public; the Abatzoglou et al. 2023 catalogue of downslope-wind fires is cited as context, its data were not reachable.

How this panel was checked
  • The event rule was fixed before looking (prereg): rarest 5 % offshore push, or a High Wind / Extreme Wind Warning or Wind Advisory; Red Flag alone does not count.
  • Pressure from one weather map (ERA5) for every year, so 2003 and 2025 are judged the same way.
  • Fires before the warning archive are marked 'unknown', never 'no'.
  • Published accounts were checked on 2026-10-14: each DOI fetched from Crossref and the abstract or report read; two were corrected (Camp: the source confirms a downslope windstorm but not the Jarbo Gap detail; Chimney Tops 2: a mountain-wave event, not downslope), and one (Keeley et al. 2004) was replaced for the 2003 fires because its readable abstract does not mention wind. They are context and do not feed the rule.
Added 2026-10-13 22:18 PDT · updated 2026-10-14 17:18 PDT

How the wind measures relate to each other

The owner asked whether these wind measures go together. Mostly yes: the windiest spot within 25 km and within 100 km rank the fires almost the same way (0.84); the town cell and the finer town maps of the earlier study agree less (0.57). How unusual the wind was for the place goes with how strong it was (0.74). Longer fires were not windier: fire length runs slightly against the wind measures (-0.28 with the windiest spot within 25 km), as wind-driven fires tend to burn their towns fast. Humidity hardly tracks wind (-0.01) but does track the offshore push (0.44): offshore winds are dry winds. The gust percentile ranks fires almost exactly like the wind percentile (0.95), so it is left out of the grid (all pairs are in the table file). Columns are numbered like the rows. What it suggests: the broader measures largely tell one story (a regional wind event), so adding more of them adds little new information.

Spearman ρ, pairwise complete over our 2002–26 record (in_R2), p31x_corr_matrix.csv. Offshore percentile and minimum humidity are sign-flipped so that higher = more extreme. axis_wmax (PA41) switches source in Oct 2024 (CONUS404 → RTMA); it is shown here only for the relationship, never in a group comparison.

Added 2026-10-13 22:18 PDT · updated 2026-10-14 17:18 PDT

Broader wind and how much was lost, all fires

More broadly, among all fires with at least 100 buildings nearby and at least one destroyed, do fires in stronger regional wind lose a larger share? Our record: rank correlation 0.00 (95% range -0.10 to 0.11, 354 fires) for the windiest spot within 100 km. For the share destroyed, 13 of 15 rows have a range that includes 0 (no clear link). For the number destroyed, the clearest link is with gusty hours over the whole fire (Carlson 2002–22 0.20 (0.10 to 0.31); Our full 2002–26 record 0.19 (0.09 to 0.29); CAL FIRE inspections 0.41 (0.22 to 0.55)). What it suggests: broader wind does not tell what share of a place burns; fires with more gusty hours destroyed more buildings in total, which also reflects their size. Wind and big losses also travel together with large fast fires, so this is a description, not a cause.

Spearman ρ with 2,000 fire-bootstrap draws (seed 20261014), p31x_loss_corr.csv; terciles p31x_loss_bins.csv. Denominators: R1/R2 exposed buildings (p24), R3 DINS-inspected buildings (p27).

Added 2026-10-13 19:05 PDT · updated 2026-10-14 17:18 PDT

Wind over the town, not at the airport (PA41)

The earlier study read wind at the nearest airport in the first two days after ignition. For the 16 named fires below, the gust over the town while it burned was higher than the airport gust for 8 of the 12 fires that have both, sometimes far higher (Eaton 2025: 8.7 m/s at the airport, 36.2 m/s over Altadena). Airports sit in valleys or far from town, and some towns burned days after ignition.

Did the fires that became urban conflagrations have stronger wind over the town? No clear difference in any record. Our full record: median 12.0 m/s for the 10 that became urban conflagrations vs 10.9 m/s for the 15 whose big block did not (p 0.85); Carlson p 0.51; CAL FIRE p 0.46. What it suggests: wind brings fire into a town, but among towns with a big block of close buildings that fire reached, wind over the town does not tell which became an urban conflagration.

A trap we avoided: older fires were measured with a product that reads peak winds about 3.4 m/s low. 10 of the 15 fires whose block did not become an urban conflagration are from before 2014, and 9 of the 10 that did are from 2014 on, so that product makes a false gap (the check rows boxed in red). The main measure uses one consistent source for every fire.

PA41, docs/ledger.d/2026-10-14-0125-town-wind--result.md. Groups use the 89-building line on the current (PA43) building set. Medians with exact 95% intervals; Mann-Whitney p (p31w_compare.csv). axis_wmax p: 0.51, 0.85, 0.46. Named fires: p31w_named.csv.

Added 2026-10-13 19:05 PDT · updated 2026-10-14 17:18 PDT

Canadian and Mexican buildings kept (PA43)

Some fires near the border reached buildings in Mexico or Canada. On 13 October we had left those buildings out. We now keep them, marked by country: 27,181 buildings around 13 border fires (26,151 in Mexico, 379 of them inside a fire area; 1,030 in Canada, 1 inside a fire area). For fires from 2016 on, our damage model looked at 23,155 of them in 11 fires; of the 6,908 that enter our building counts, it calls none destroyed (it calls 19 others destroyed, in Granjeno 2023: 1, Border 6 2025: 18, but those are map points without a building outline and enter no count). For older fires we cannot tell, and count them as not destroyed. The table shows the three ways side by side. The two 'all buildings' ways agree exactly.

Harris 2007: did the Mexican block burn? The fire's hand-drawn outline runs along the border, so a block of 141 buildings in Tecate, Mexico, counts as reached by the fire. A satellite check says the ground there did not burn: 0 of the 141 buildings show a burn signal (Landsat burn index, before vs after the fire, at least 0.10; median 0.007), and 0 of 121 other Mexican buildings inside the outline. On the U.S. side of the same fire, 148 of the 165 buildings Carlson marks destroyed show it. This checks whether the ground around each building burned, in 30 m squares; it is a burn-index check, not a damage label for the buildings.

What it means: no conclusion changed. In every record and every way, no fire whose biggest block of close buildings held 89 or fewer became an urban conflagration. Keeping the buildings puts Harris 2007 back above the line (its block grows from 42 to 141), but that is because of the outline, not because the Mexican block burned.

Foreign outcome: Border 3 2016 production first call (damage_sentinel2_final_v1, cut 0.88); Border 32 2022 and Caribou 2017 leave-one-fire-out, 4 seeds; before 2016 unknown → not destroyed. Harris check: Landsat 7 median of 4 clear scenes before and 4 after, dNBR 3 × 3 mean at each building (p24_harris_mexico_dnbr.csv); Landsat 5 pair three months later 0 of 141. U.S. side: destroyed 148 of 165 (median 0.20), surviving 526 of 1428.

Added 2026-10-13 16:54 PDT · updated 2026-10-14 17:18 PDT

Trees between the houses of the biggest block

Of the 25 fires in our 2002–26 record that reached a block of more than 89 closely spaced buildings, 10 became urban conflagrations (at least 50 destroyed buildings in one connected patch). Tree canopy between the houses was not higher in those 10: median 10.9% vs 12.0% in the 14 that did not (p 0.71). The share of house-to-house links passing through trees was 7% vs 0% (p 0.49). The other two records agree. What it suggests: trees between houses do not explain which big blocks became urban conflagrations.T1 (prereg PA36): primary measures G1 (mean canopy at link midpoints) and G2_25 (share of links with midpoint canopy ≥ 25%), USFS Science TCC v2025-6 at ignition year − 2 (year − 1 failed the leak check). Exact or 200,000-draw permutation tests on the difference of medians, Holm over {G1, G2}; bar Holm p < 0.05 in R2 with the same sign in R1 and R3: not shown. Supporting Firth logit (R2, ≥ 100 exposed, n 353, 10 events): adding standardised G1 to log10(1 + block) gives LR p 0.23; leave-one-fire-out AUC 0.985 → 0.982 (Δ CI -0.012 to +0.001).

Added 2026-10-13 16:54 PDT · updated 2026-10-14 17:18 PDT

Does a 'fuel-linked' block predict better?

Linking houses through trees (up to 60 m apart, with canopy all the way between) does not predict better than buildings alone. In our 2002–26 record (726 fires, 10 conflagrations) the ranking score went from 0.992 to 0.990, and the rule caught the same 10 conflagrations with 23 false alarms instead of 15. What it suggests: keep the building-only definition; trees mostly add forest towns that did not become an urban conflagration.T2: Firth logit on log10(1 + FLB_25_60) vs log10(1 + biggest block), leave-one-fire-out AUC and mean log score; paired fire bootstrap (2,000) of ΔAUC. Bar 'better' = higher log score in all three records and R2 ΔAUC CI above 0: no better. Sensitivities (canopy ≥ 50%, reach 80 m, year − 1, ≥ 100 exposed) are in docs/paper/tables/p30_t2_flb.csv; none passes the bar.

Big losses in sparse, treed housing

Below the line (the 330 fires with ≥ 100 exposed buildings whose biggest block is ≤ 89), fires with more tree canopy around houses lost a larger share of them, but only weakly (rank correlation 0.25). Of the 37 big sparse losses (≥ 300 destroyed), 3 form a chain of 50+ destroyed buildings only when links through trees are allowed. Gatlinburg (Chimney Tops 2, 2016) is the clearest: 1,517 destroyed, never more than 16 within 30 m of each other, but 326 joined through continuous tree canopy. What it suggests: in forested towns, trees can carry fire between houses that are too far apart to ignite each other; that is a different kind of town loss from a dense urban conflagration.T3 (descriptive): Spearman of G3a (canopy within 30 m of exposed buildings) with destroyed share 0.25 [0.14, 0.35], with the largest destroyed chain at 50 m 0.20 [0.10, 0.31], n 330 (R2, biggest block ≤ 89, ≥ 100 exposed). Fuel-linked destroyed chain FLDC = destroyed links ≤ 30 m or 30–60 m with every 10 m canopy sample ≥ 25%; the plain 60 m chain shows what reach alone gives (Erskine, Dixie: long chains, but not through trees). Outcome-side and descriptive; the definition itself is PA34's study.

Wind: most were wind events

Newer measure above: the panel “Wind over the town, not at the airport” reads the wind over each town while it burned; this panel keeps the earlier airport gusts for comparison. Added 2026-10-13 16:54 PDT · updated 2026-10-14 17:18 PDT

What others found about trees, fences and wind between houses

Field studies agree with what we see: the spacing of buildings comes first; vegetation near a house matters for that house and inside a burning town, but adds little to explain which towns become urban conflagrations. Fences and other small fuels are a known path from house to house in experiments and NIST case studies, but no study maps them at the scale needed here. No peer-reviewed Lahaina study with a DOI was found that measures trees or fences between buildings.Every DOI resolved on Crossref on 2026-10-13; claims come from the abstracts (reports without abstracts are cited for their scope only).

TopicReferenceDOIWhat it saysWhy it matters here
trees and spacingKnapp, Valachovic, Quarles et al. 2021, Fire Ecology10.1186/s42408-021-00117-0Camp Fire 2018, sampled single-family homes: distance to the nearest destroyed structure, the number destroyed within 100 m and pre-fire overstory canopy cover within 100 m were the strongest predictors of survival; homes more than 18 m from a destroyed structure and with under 53% canopy at 30-100 m survived at higher rates.House-to-house spacing first; canopy matters inside a burning town
vegetation near housesSyphard, Brennan & Keeley 2014, International Journal of Wildland Fire10.1071/WF13158San Diego County fires 2001-2010, 1,000 destroyed vs 1,000 surviving structures on pre-fire air photos: defensible space next to the structure helped, most effectively at 5-20 m.Vegetation right next to a house matters for that house
building arrangementSyphard, Keeley, Massada et al. 2012, PLoS ONE10.1371/journal.pone.0033954Housing arrangement and location determine the likelihood of housing loss to wildfire (title claim).Arrangement of buildings is the first-order factor
vegetation vs building featuresSyphard & Keeley 2019, Fire10.3390/fire203004940,000+ inspected structures 2013-2018 in California: building features (enclosed eaves, vent screens, multi-pane windows) explained more than defensible-space distance; many 'fire-safe' structures were still destroyed.Vegetation is a modest factor once a fire reaches homes
vegetation vs arrangementSyphard, Rustigian-Romsos & Keeley 2021, Fire10.3390/fire4010012The pattern of housing relative to vegetation explained structure loss better than the local amount of vegetation (NDVI).Agrees with buildings-first
very fine pre-fire land coverMockrin, Locke, Syphard et al. 2023, Journal of Environmental Management10.1016/j.jenvman.2023.118960Woolsey Fire 2018 with 0.07 m2 pre-fire land cover: vegetation around buildings was not a strong predictor of building damage compared with building materials, paved cover, building density and distance to roads.Even very sharp pre-fire canopy maps add little in a burning suburb
case study (Camp)Maranghides, Link, Mell et al. 2021, NIST Technical Note 213510.6028/NIST.TN.2135Camp Fire progression timeline through Paradise (report; no abstract on Crossref).Documents the wind and the spread through town
case study (Witch)Maranghides & Mell 2009, NIST Technical Note 163510.6028/NIST.TN.1635Witch and Guejito fires: case study of a community (Trails) (report).One of the 15 big-block fires that did not become an urban conflagration
case study (Witch) 2Maranghides, McNamara, Mell et al. 2013, NIST Technical Note 179610.6028/NIST.TN.1796Witch and Guejito fires report 2: effects of hazard mitigation actions on structure ignition (report).Mitigation and defensive actions in a big block that did not become an urban conflagration
case study (Waldo)Maranghides, McNamara, Vihnanek et al. 2015, NIST Technical Note 191010.6028/NIST.TN.1910Waldo Canyon Fire 2012: event timeline and defensive actions in Mountain Shadows (report).Outside conflagration in our tests

exposure pathwaysCaton, Hakes, Gorham et al. 2016, Fire Technology (Part I)10.1007/s10694-016-0589-zReview of exposure conditions (embers, radiation, flame contact) in WUI building fire spread.Physical basis for building-to-building spread
combustibles near housesSuzuki & Manzello 2021, Sustainability10.3390/su13042136Experiments: combustibles around houses (e.g. wood decking and mulch) can ignite in similar times under firebrand showers.Small fuels between houses can carry fire
hazard methodologyMaranghides, Link, Hawks et al. 2022, NIST Technical Note 220510.6028/NIST.TN.2205WUI structure-parcel-community hazard mitigation methodology built from post-fire field observations: exposures from embers and from fire (radiation, convection).Treats parcel fuels between structures as exposure sources
community fire spread modelMahmoud & Chulahwat 2018, Scientific Reports10.1038/s41598-018-27215-5A graph model of fire spread through a community, with wind, layout and structure-to-structure modes.Network view of building chains

wind (2017)Nauslar, Abatzoglou & Marsh 2018, Fire10.3390/fire1010018October 2017 North Bay fires with strong downslope winds; December 2017 southern California fires in the longest Santa Ana event on record.Tubbs, Sulfur, Thomas, Creek 2017, Lilac
